conceptTag: Franchise a gym or go independent?
readerTitle: Should a great trainer buy a gym franchise?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (개인 트레이너의 피트니스 스튜디오 창업, 소규모 사무실 대상 IT 지원 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 프랜차이즈는 검증된 시스템을 빌리는 것이므로, 내가 못 하는 부분을 그 시스템이 채워 줄 때만 수수료만큼의 값을 한다. 어느 길을 가든 오너의 시간이 어디로 갈지는 따로 계산해야 한다.
misconception: 프랜차이즈는 원래 더 안전하고, 사업이 알아서 돌아가게 해 준다. 또는 실력이 좋으면 독립하는 게 당연히 낫다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨: ENT-02-06 (프랜차이즈 vs 독립), ENT-02-04 (오너의 시간 함정)
모든 수치와 인물은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산: 월매출 $40,000 × 로열티 6% = $2,400, × 마케팅 분담금 2% = $800, 합계 월 $3,200, 연 $38,400.
추가 회원 계산: $3,200 ÷ 월 회비 $100 = 32명. 추가 회원 매출에도 8% 수수료가 붙으므로 실제로는 $3,200 ÷ $92 ≈ 35명이 필요합니다. 카드에는 "more than 30 extra members"로 적었습니다.
프랜차이즈 계약 조건(영업 지역, 갱신, 매각 제한 등)은 나라와 브랜드마다 다릅니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 일반적인 표현만 썼습니다.

cards.title: Should a great trainer buy a gym franchise?
body: Maya has coached clients for eight years. Her calendar is full, and she has savings for her own studio.
Two offers sit on her desk. A fitness franchise will hand her a brand, a floor plan and a booking system. Or she can open under her own name. Same city, same savings. Very different businesses.

image.label: A trainer holding two keys at a crossroads
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 운동복 차림의 트레이너가 열쇠 두 개를 들고 갈림길에 서 있음. 왼쪽 길 끝에는 똑같은 간판이 줄지어 선 체인 헬스장, 오른쪽 길 끝에는 손글씨 간판의 작은 스튜디오. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Maya figure out first?
body: She has a week to decide. Where should she start?

options.text: Compare the franchise fees with what the independent studio would cost to set up
options.feedback: Costs matter, but a fee is only expensive or cheap next to what it buys. Without knowing what she's buying, the comparison has no anchor.

options.text: List what the franchise gives her that she can't do well herself, and what she gives up for it
options.feedback: This is **franchise vs independent** at work. A franchise is a rented system. It's worth paying for only where it fills a real gap.

options.text: Go independent. She's a skilled coach, so she doesn't need someone else's playbook
options.feedback: Coaching skill runs the sessions, not the business. Marketing, pricing and staffing are separate skills, and that's exactly what a franchise sells.

cards.title: What the system costs each year.
body: Say her studio brings in $40,000 a month. On top of an upfront fee, the franchise takes a share of every month's sales.
The real question: will the brand and playbook bring in more than **$38,400 a year** she wouldn't earn alone? At $100 a month per member, that's more than 30 extra members.

cards.title: She's renting a system. Does it fill her gap?
body: Maya writes it down honestly. Strong: coaching, keeping clients. Weak: marketing, pricing, choosing equipment, building a sign-up process.
The franchise covers most of her weak side. But her strength is loyal clients who already know *her* name, and a big brand could blur that.
So the answer isn't "franchises are safer." It's **whether this system covers the gaps she actually has**, at a price below what those gaps would cost her.

image.label: Two columns: Maya's strengths vs what the franchise provides
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 열 "Maya is strong at": Coaching, Keeping clients. 오른쪽 열 "Franchise provides": Brand, Marketing, Floor plan, Booking system. 겹치는 부분 없이 오른쪽이 왼쪽의 빈 곳을 채우는 퍼즐 모양으로 표현.

cards.softwareNote: Software agencies face the same call when joining a vendor's partner program. The badge and leads cost a revenue share or sales quotas. It pays off only if finding clients is the agency's real gap.

cards.title: Maya leans independent. Check her plan.
body: To keep costs low, she plans to coach 25 sessions a week herself and run everything else in the gaps. What's the weak spot?

options.text: Nothing. Coaching herself saves a trainer's wages
options.feedback: She saves wages but loses the hours for sales, hiring, cleaning and books. When she's sick, revenue stops.

options.text: She hasn't planned hours for running the business. Budget them, and hire a second coach early
options.feedback: This is **the owner's time trap**. If every session needs her, the studio can't grow past her calendar.

options.text: Choose the franchise instead, because the system runs itself
options.feedback: A playbook saves design work, but someone still has to run it. Many franchises expect the owner on site, so the hours don't disappear.

cards.title: Read the fine print and call the owners.
body: A franchise agreement can limit where you open, what you sell, how you renew and who you can sell the business to later. Have someone qualified read it.
Your fate is also tied to the brand. If other locations get bad reviews, your members see them too.
The most useful research is simple: call several current franchise owners. Ask how many hours they work and whether they'd sign again.

image.label: A thick contract next to a phone list of franchise owners
image.brief: 책상 위에 두꺼운 계약서와 형광펜, 옆에 "Call current owners"라고 적힌 메모와 전화기. 계약서 표지에 실제 브랜드명이나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support firm.
body: Dev fixes computers and networks for 40 small offices, all from referrals. He answers every call himself and works most evenings.
A national IT network offers its brand, ticketing tools and vendor discounts for a share of his revenue. What should he do?

options.text: Join. A national brand will bring more clients
options.feedback: Clients aren't his gap. Referrals already keep him full. More clients would deepen his **time trap**.

options.text: Stay independent, and spend the money on a second technician and his own ticketing tool
options.feedback: His gap is time, not customers. A system he doesn't need costs more than one he builds for his real problem.

options.text: Join, because the ticketing tools will save him hours
options.feedback: Tools help, but he can buy them alone for far less than a revenue share. Ask what only the network can give him.

cards.title: Pay for a system only where it fills your gap, and plan your own hours either way.
list: **Franchise vs independent:** you're renting a tested system. Match what it provides to what you lack.
**The owner's time trap:** count the hours for running the business, not just doing the work.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write two lists: what your business needs done, and what you do well. Every gap is something you'll buy, hire or learn.
